[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing intermittent fasting plus behavioral reinforcement (e.g., habit-based coaching, self-monitoring, contingency management) versus intermittent fasting alone over 12-18 months, with adherence tracking and weight outcomes as primary endpoints. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating the effect of added behavioral reinforcement on long-term adherence, compensatory eating, and weight maintenance, addressing the tension that standalone fasting may fail due to motivational and hormonal factors.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal observational study or secondary analysis of existing weight loss trials examining the relationship between adherence to intermittent fasting, measures of compensatory eating (e.g., binge eating scales, dietary recall), and weight regain beyond 12 months, with behavioral support as a moderating variable. — Provides real-world evidence on whether behavioral reinforcement attenuates the natural decline in adherence and the rise in compensatory eating over time, helping to confirm or refute the causal mechanism proposed in the hypothesis.

scope.domain: long-term (>12 months) weight maintenance with behavioral support

qualifier.tension: Behavioral reinforcement may counteract the adherence drop and hormonal hunger adaptations that undermine the initial calorie deficit in standalone intermittent fasting.

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2 or time-restricted feeding) with continuous calorie restriction over 12–24 months, measuring changes in insulin sensitivity (HOMA-IR) and body weight maintenance. — Direct, long-term RCT evidence is needed to confirm whether intermittent fasting specifically enhances metabolic flexibility and insulin sensitivity in a way that produces sustained weight loss beyond one year, compared to standard dietary approaches.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies on intermittent fasting and metabolic biomarkers (e.g., insulin sensitivity, glucose tolerance, fatty acid oxidation) in adults with overweight or obesity. — A comprehensive synthesis of existing observational and interventional data can clarify the consistency and magnitude of the hypothesized metabolic benefits, and whether they translate to durable weight loss maintenance across diverse populations.

[PATH:empirical] Mechanistic study using continuous glucose monitors and metabolic chamber assessments to track daily patterns of glucose, insulin, and fat oxidation in participants practicing intermittent fasting versus ad libitum eating over a 12-month period. — This approach would provide direct evidence for the claimed enhancement of metabolic flexibility (e.g., improved fat oxidation during fasting states) and its temporal relationship with long-term weight stability, addressing the mechanistic underpinning of the hypothesis.
